See also: Appendix:Variations of "vare"

Danish

Alternative forms

Dialectal forms
  • vare (Lollandsk, Sydfalstersk)
  • vere (Nordsjællandsk)

Etymology

All forms except the present are from Old Danish wæræ, waræ, from Old Norse vera, vesa, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell, live, reside”).

The present tense is derived from a different root: Proto-Germanic *izum, *izud, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”), which is also the origin of English is, are, Latin sum, and German ist. In Scandinavian, the singular has taken over the stem of the plural (with -z- > -r-).

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /ˈvɛːrə/, [ˈʋɛːɐ]

Verb

være (present tense er, past tense var, perfect tense har været)

  1. (copulative) to be (expresses identity between the subject and a predicative)
    Kierkegaard er en berømt filosof.
    Kierkegaard is a famous philosopher.
  2. (intransitive) to be, exist (with an adverbial phrase and/or the dummy subject der)
    På kontoret var (der) 15 ansatte.
    There were 15 employees in the office.
  3. (intransitive) to be (in cleft sentences emphasizing a noun phrase, with the dummy subject det and a relative clause)
    Det er Anders der har spist kagen.
    It was Anders who ate the cake.
  4. (auxiliary) to be (passive perfect tense with the past participle)
    Huset er bygget af træ.
    The house is built from wood.
  5. (auxiliary) to have (active perfect tense with the past participle of certain intransitive verbs)
    Synonym: have (used with most words)
    Pigen er løbet væk.
    The girl has run away.

Norwegian Bokmål

Pronunciation

  • IPA(key): /²ʋæːrə/, [ˈʋæ̂ːɾə̌]
  • Rhymes: -æːrə
  • Homophone: Være
  • Hyphenation: væ‧re

Etymology 1

Inherited from Middle Norwegian vera (“to be”), from Old Norse vera, earlier vesa, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”).[1] The infinitive and past-tense stem continue Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell; stay”). The present tense er, from Old Norse er, earlier es, belongs to the suppletive present-tense paradigm ultimately inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”).

Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vere, Danish være, Swedish vara, Icelandic vera, Faroese vera, Dutch wezen (“to be”), and English was and were.

Verb

være (imperative vær, present tense er, simple past var, supine vært, past participle vært, present participle værende, verbal noun væren)

  1. (copulative) to be; to have a particular identity, classification, quality or condition.[2]
    Søsteren min er lærer. ― My sister is a teacher.
    Barna er trøtte. ― The children are tired.
    Bordet er av eik. ― The table is made of oak.
    Hun er fra Bergen. ― She is from Bergen.
    Klokka er halv ni. ― It is half past eight.
    Tre og fire er sju. ― Three and four are seven.
    vær så snill — please
    Vær så snill og lukk vinduet. ― Please close the window.
    vær så god — here you are; help yourself; you're welcome
    Vær så god, her er kaffen din. ― Here you are; here is your coffee.
    • 1886, Henrik Ibsen, Rosmersholm‎, act 1, page 14:
      Han er fem år yngre end jeg.
      He is five years younger than I am.
    1. To play or act as a character or assumed identity.[3]
      I skoleforestillingen skal jeg være kongen. ― In the school play, I am going to play the king.
  2. (intransitive) to be, exist; of a person, to live.
    Synonyms: eksistere, finnes
    Det er fortsatt håp. ― There is still hope.
    være til — to exist
    Hun var glad for å være til. ― She was glad to be alive.
    ikke være mer — to be dead; to no longer exist
    være eller ikke være — to be or not to be; to survive or perish
    • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, act 4, page 155:
      Der er visse krav
      There are certain demands
  3. (intransitive) to be, stay; to be situated somewhere or in a particular situation.
    Vi er på biblioteket. ― We are at the library.
    De var i en vanskelig situasjon. ― They were in a difficult situation.
    Jeg er hos deg om ti minutter. ― I will be with you in ten minutes.
    bli værende — to stay, remain
    Hun ble værende hos oss til søndag. ― She stayed with us until Sunday.
    være med — to come along; to participate
    Vil du være med på turen? ― Would you like to come along on the trip?
    være med på — to participate in; to agree to
    Jeg er med på forslaget. ― I agree to the proposal.
    være ute etter — to seek; to be after
    Hva er du ute etter? ― What are you after?
    • 1886, Henrik Ibsen, Rosmersholm‎, act 1, page 5:
      Nej, han er ude og går.
      No, he is out walking.
  4. (intransitive) to take place, occur; to be held.
    Synonyms: finne sted, foregå
    Konserten skal være i gymsalen. ― The concert will take place in the gymnasium.
    • 1880, Alexander L. Kielland, “En Middag”, in Novelletter‎, 2nd edition:
      Der var stor Middag hos Grossereren.
      There was a grand dinner at the merchant’s house.
  5. (intransitive) to remain; to be left unchanged or undisturbed.
    La papirene være til i morgen. ― Leave the papers until tomorrow.
    la noen/noe være — to leave someone or something alone
    La hunden være mens den spiser. ― Leave the dog alone while it is eating.
    la være — to refrain; to desist
    Jeg lot være å svare. ― I refrained from answering.
    det får være — never mind; it will have to wait
    det får så være — so be it
    • 1885, Amalie Skram, chapter IX, in Constance Ring‎, page 155:
      Lad mig være, Menneske,
      Leave me alone, man,
  6. (intransitive) to behave, act; to fare or be the case.
    Hun kan være vanskelig når hun er trøtt. ― She can be difficult when she is tired.
    Hvordan er det med faren din? ― How is your father doing?
    Slik er det ikke lenger. ― That is no longer the case.
    • 1920, Jonas Lie, “Tremasteren «Fremtiden», chapter XIII”, in Samlede Digterverker‎, volume I, page 280:
      En naturlig Maade at være paa eller et lykkeligt Ord fra hans Side vilde have skaffet Luft for dette; […]
      A natural manner or a well-chosen word from him would have cleared the air about this; […]
  7. (copulative) to mean, entail, amount to.[2]
    Å gi opp nå er å kaste bort alt arbeidet. ― Giving up now means throwing away all the work.
  8. To be, used with a dummy subject, particularly in impersonal and cleft constructions.[2]
    Det er kaldt ute. ― It is cold outside.
    Det var Kari som fant nøkkelen. ― It was Kari who found the key.
    Det er på fredag vi reiser. ― It is on Friday that we are leaving.
  9. (auxiliary) to have; used with a past participle to form perfect tenses of certain verbs of motion or change of state.
    Gjestene er kommet. ― The guests have arrived.
    Da vi våknet, var snøen smeltet. ― When we woke up, the snow had melted.
    • 1886, Henrik Ibsen, Rosmersholm‎, act 1, page 18:
      For nu er oprørsånden trængt ind i selve skolen.
      For now the spirit of rebellion has penetrated the school itself.
  10. (auxiliary) to be; used with a past participle to form a passive construction, often expressing a resulting state.
    Alle billettene er solgt. ― All the tickets have been sold.
    Døra var låst. ― The door was locked.
    • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, act 4, page 150:
      Der har nylig været fotograferet
      Photographs have recently been taken
  11. (subjunctive) to be; used in wishes, blessings and concessive expressions.[3]
    Ære være dem som hjalp til. ― Honour be to those who helped.
    det være seg — whether; be it
    Alle kan bidra, det være seg med tid eller penger. ― Everyone can contribute, whether with time or money.
    takket være — thanks to
    Vi rakk toget takket være hjelpen din. ― We caught the train thanks to your help.
    • 2021 April 15, Slemmestad og Nærsnes menighet, “Liturgirevisjon”, in (Please provide the book title or journal name)‎:
      Guds fred være med dere.
      God’s peace be with you.
Usage notes
  • The finite forms do not vary with the subject's person or number: er is used throughout the present tense and var throughout the past tense.
  • The perfect of this verb itself uses ha: har vært (“has/have been”).
  • With verbs of motion or change of state, ha and være may both occur as perfect auxiliaries. Constructions with være often emphasize the resulting state.
  • The subjunctive være survives chiefly in established expressions. The ordinary imperative is vær.
  • A repeated noun on either side of the verb can emphasize its usual implications: Et løfte er et løfte (“A promise is a promise”).
Derived terms
  • fravær (“absence”)
  • fraværende (“absent”)
  • gjenværende (“remaining”)
  • nærvær (“presence”)
  • nåværende (“current; present”)
  • overvære (“to attend; witness”)
  • samvær (“time spent together; company”)
  • unnvære (“to do without”)
  • væremåte (“manner; demeanour”)
  • værested (“place to stay; meeting place”)

Etymology 2

Inherited from Old Norse viðra (“to blow; scent”), from Proto-Germanic *wedrōną (“to expose to the weather”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *wedrą (“weather”), whose further origin is uncertain. Related to vær (“weather”).

Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vêre, Danish vejre (“to scent”), Swedish vädra (“to air; scent”), Icelandic viðra (“to air; ventilate”), and German wettern (“to storm; rant”).

Verb

være (imperative vær, present tense værer, passive væres, simple past været or væra, supine været or væra, past participle været or væra, present participle værende, verbal noun væring)

  1. (intransitive) to sniff, especially to investigate a scent.
    Synonym: snuse
    Hunden løftet hodet og været mot vinden. ― The dog raised its head and sniffed into the wind.
    • 1989, Tove Nilsen, Chaplins hemmelighet, page 145:
      en hjort som været med våte nesebor
      a deer sniffing with wet nostrils
  2. (transitive) to scent, smell; to detect by smell.
    Reven hadde været maten på lang avstand. ― The fox had scented the food from far away.
    • 2004, Thorvald Steen, Kamelskyer:
      kameler kan være en fremmed på en kilometers avstand
      camels can scent a stranger from a kilometre away
  3. (transitive, figurative) to sense, anticipate, get wind of.
    Synonym: ane
    Journalisten været en skandale. ― The journalist sensed a scandal.
    • 1875, Henrik Ibsen, Digte, page 122:
      kløgtig skytte faren vejrer
      the shrewd marksman senses danger
  4. (intransitive, figurative) to seek, yearn for or anticipate something, especially with etter or mot.[4]
    • 1925, Sigrid Undset, Olav Audunssøn i Hestviken, volume I, page 58:
      […] alle tok til at veire mot forandring og storhændinger
      […] everyone began looking forward to change and momentous events
    Alle været mot forandring. ― Everyone was looking forward to change.
  5. (literary) to blow away, disperse, often with an adverb.[5]
    • 1875, Henrik Ibsen, Catilina, page 78:
      Kapitol skal vejres fra sin højde
      The Capitol shall be blown from its height.
    Vinden været støvet bort. ― The wind blew the dust away.
    1. (figurative) to destroy, obliterate.[6]
      Krigen været bort deres siste håp. ― The war swept away their last hope.
      • 1875, Henrik Ibsen, Digte, page 67:
        sent skal tidens storme vejre bort din sagas sejre!
        Not soon shall the storms of time sweep away the triumphs of your saga!

Etymology 3

Nominalization of være (“to be”).

Compare Norwegian Nynorsk være (“existence; place to stay”).

Noun

være n

  1. being, existence.[2]
    Synonyms: eksistens, tilværelse, væren
    Han lengtet etter et fredelig være. ― He longed for a peaceful existence.
    • 1883, N. A. Dahl, Gud og Verden‎, Bergen: C. Floor, page 38:
      Skabningen har sit Være af og i Gud og er derfor ogsaa selv Aand.
      Creation has its being from and in God and is therefore itself also spirit.
  2. (rare) a stay, sojourn.[7]
    Synonym: opphold
    Hans være i byen ble kortvarig. ― His stay in the town was brief.
Usage notes

As a final element in compounds, the noun also occurs with meanings of possession or custody.[8]

Derived terms
  • husvære (“lodging; accommodation”)
  • velvære (“well-being”)
